title: Planar Linear Arboricity Conjecture (Conjecture 1)
statement_text: For any planar graph $G$ of maximum degree $\Delta \geq 5$, we have $\mathrm{la}(G) = \left\lceil \frac{\Delta}{2} \right\rceil$.
context_text: Cygan et al. proved $\mathrm{la}(G) = \lceil \Delta/2 \rceil$ for planar graphs with $\Delta \geq 9$ and posed this conjecture extending that result to all $\Delta \geq 5$. The conjecture implies the Vizing Planar Graph Conjecture, which is currently open only for $\Delta = 6$.
paper_contribution: Proves Conjecture 2 (a refined partition result) for $\Delta = 9$, showing that edges of any planar graph with $\Delta(G) \leq 9$ can be partitioned into 4 linear forests and a matching; combined with Theorem 1, this yields $\mathrm{la}(G) = \lceil \Delta/2 \rceil$ for all planar $G$ with odd $\Delta \geq 9$ via a matching-augmented decomposition.
paper_title: Partitioning edges of a planar graph into linear forests and a matching

title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: For every planar graph $G$ of odd maximum degree $\Delta \geq 7$ the edges of $G$ can be partitioned into $\frac{\Delta-1}{2}$ linear forests and one matching.
context_text: A linear forest is a forest whose components are paths, and the linear arboricity $\mathrm{la}(G)$ is the minimum number of linear forests whose union is $G$. For planar graphs, $\mathrm{la}(G)\le\lceil(\Delta+1)/2\rceil$ (Wu, and Wu and Wu), and Cygan et al. proved $\mathrm{la}(G)=\lceil\Delta/2\rceil$ when $\Delta\ge9$ and conjectured it for $\Delta\ge5$. For odd $\Delta$ the equality $\mathrm{la}(G)=\lceil\Delta/2\rceil$ already holds, which leaves freedom (each vertex has a linear forest with at most one incident edge) that the conjecture tries to exploit by replacing one linear forest by a matching. The conjecture implies chromatic index $\Delta$ (colour each linear forest with two colours and the matching with one more), so it fails for $\Delta\in\{3,5\}$ ($K_4$ and the icosahedron with one edge subdivided). It holds for $\Delta\ge11$ by combining Vizing's theorem that planar graphs with $\Delta\ge8$ have chromatic index $\Delta$ (remove one colour class, a matching) with the result of Cygan et al. The paper proves that every planar graph of maximum degree at most $9$ can be partitioned into $4$ linear forests and a matching, settling $\Delta=9$; the case $\Delta=7$ remains open (it would strengthen the result of Sanders and Zhao that planar graphs of maximum degree $7$ have chromatic index $7$), and the authors think it needs a different, more global argument.
paper_title: Partitioning edges of a planar graph into linear forests and a matching
